1.lecture:
§1 · Four words that are not synonyms

A measurement is a claim about the world, and like any claim it can be wrong in more than one way. Quality work depends on separating the ways, because each has a different cure and confusing them wastes money on the wrong one.

Resolution is the smallest change an instrument can display — 1 µm on a digital micrometer, 0.02 mm on a vernier caliper. It is a property of the display, and it is the weakest of the four: an instrument can resolve to a micrometre and be wrong by fifty.

Precision, or repeatability, is how closely repeated measurements of the same thing agree with each other. It is measured as a standard deviation and improved by technique, fixturing and averaging.

Bias is the systematic difference between the average of many measurements and the true value. It does not shrink with repetition, and no amount of care in the measuring reduces it.

Accuracy is closeness to the true value, and it needs both: small bias and small scatter. The figure shows the case that catches people out — ten readings of a certified 25.0000 mm block, scattering by only about a micrometre, all of them about five micrometres too big. The instrument is precise and inaccurate, and the operator who checks repeatability and stops there will believe it is fine.

§2 · What the readings actually say

Take the ten readings, in micrometres above the certified value: 4, 6, 5, 7, 4, 6, 5, 6, 4, 5.

Key relations — separating scatter from offset

\[ \bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum x_i,\qquad s=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1}},\qquad \text{bias}=\bar{x}-x_{\text{ref}},\qquad u(\bar{x})=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \]

\( s \) is the spread of a single reading; \( s/\sqrt{n} \) is the uncertainty of their mean. Bias is the distance from that mean to the reference and is not divided by anything.

The mean is 5.2 µm, so the instrument reads 25.0052 mm against a block certified at 25.0000. The sample standard deviation is 1.03 µm. Averaging ten readings tightens the mean to \( 1.03/\sqrt{10}=0.33\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) — genuinely worth having — while the 5.2 µm bias is untouched. That asymmetry is the whole practical point: repetition buys precision and never buys accuracy.

The block itself carries an uncertainty, quoted on its certificate as \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( k=2 \). Compare that with the 5.2 µm bias and the verdict is unambiguous: the reference is twenty-six times better than the error being measured, so the error belongs to the micrometer. Had the two been comparable, the honest conclusion would have been that the check could not resolve the question.

§3 · Traceability: why anyone should believe the block

The block's certificate is only worth what stands behind it. Traceability is that chain: an unbroken sequence of calibrations, each with its own stated uncertainty, linking a working instrument to a national measurement institute and through it to the SI definition of the metre.

Each link degrades slightly — uncertainty accumulates downward, never shrinks — which is why a working gauge is calibrated against a reference gauge several times better than itself, rather than against another working gauge. The usual guidance is a ratio of at least 4:1 between the tolerance being checked and the uncertainty of the check, and the 26:1 above is comfortable.

A calibration certificate is readable once the vocabulary is: the measurand is what was measured, the reference standard is what it was measured against and where its traceability comes from, the result is a value with an uncertainty and a coverage factor, the conditions are the temperature and humidity it holds at, and the statement of conformity is a judgement against a specification, not a measurement. A certificate with a result and no uncertainty is not a calibration certificate.

§4 · Temperature, the error nobody writes on the drawing

Dimensional metrology is defined at 20°C. That is not a nicety; it is part of what a length means, because every material changes size with temperature.

Key relation — thermal error

\[ \Delta L=L\,\alpha\,\Delta T \]

\( \alpha \approx 11.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} \) for steel and \( 23.1\times10^{-6} \) for aluminium.

A 200 mm steel part measured in a 25°C workshop instead of a 20°C room is \( 200(11.5\times10^{-6})(5) = 11.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) longer than its defined size. On an IT7 tolerance of about 46 µm that is a quarter of the band, spent before any instrument is picked up. The same part in aluminium moves 23.1 µm.

Two consequences follow. First, the difference between materials matters as much as the absolute movement: measuring an aluminium part with a steel gauge at 25°C leaves \( 23.1-11.5 = 11.6\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) of differential expansion that no amount of instrument quality removes. Second, soak time is a real requirement rather than a ritual — a part carried from a machine to an inspection room is not at room temperature when it arrives, and measuring it immediately measures its history rather than its size.
1.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Mean and standard deviation (Engineering Statistics L2) — the two numbers that separate scatter from offset.
  • The standard error of a mean (Engineering Statistics L5) — \( s/\sqrt{n} \), and what it does and does not improve.
  • Thermal expansion (Materials Science I L6) — \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \), applied here at micrometre scale.
  • Tolerances and IT grades (Engineering Drawing & CAD L6) — the bands these errors are being spent against.
  • SI units (Engineering Mathematics I L1) — the definition the traceability chain terminates at.

quiz.q:
Separating precision from accuracy

Problem. A micrometer is used ten times on a gauge block certified at 25.0000 mm with \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) (\( k=2 \)). The readings, in micrometres above the certified value, are 4, 6, 5, 7, 4, 6, 5, 6, 4, 5. Find the mean reading, the repeatability standard deviation, the bias, and the uncertainty of the mean. State whether the instrument is precise, accurate, both or neither.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \bar{x} = (4+6+5+7+4+6+5+6+4+5)/10 = 52/10 = 5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so the mean reading is 25.0052 mm.

(2) Deviations from 5.2: −1.2, 0.8, −0.2, 1.8, −1.2, 0.8, −0.2, 0.8, −1.2, −0.2. Their squares sum to 9.60, so \( s = \sqrt{9.60/9} = \sqrt{1.0667} = 1.03\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) Bias \( = 5.2 - 0 = +5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \): the instrument reads high.

(4) \( u(\bar{x}) = s/\sqrt{n} = 1.03/\sqrt{10} = 0.33\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

Answer: mean 25.0052 mm, \( s = 1.03\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), bias \( +5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), \( u(\bar{x}) = 0.33\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The instrument is precise but not accurate. Sanity check: the bias is 5.2 µm against a reference uncertainty of 0.2 µm — a ratio of 26, so the error is unambiguously the micrometer's and not the block's. Note what averaging did and did not do: it reduced the uncertainty of the mean to 0.33 µm, better than a single reading by a factor of \( \sqrt{10} \), while leaving the 5.2 µm error exactly where it was. Precision is earned by repetition; accuracy is earned by calibration.

quiz.q:
Thermal error against the tolerance band (with a US customary check)

Problem. A 200 mm shaft is measured in a workshop at 25°C rather than the reference 20°C. Find the thermal error for steel (\( \alpha = 11.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} \)) and for aluminium (\( 23.1\times10^{-6} \)), express the steel error as a fraction of an IT7 tolerance of 46 µm, and give the steel error in thousandths of an inch. Then state the error left if an aluminium part is measured with a steel gauge at that temperature.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Steel: \( \Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T = 200(11.5\times10^{-6})(5) = 0.0115\ \mathrm{mm} = 11.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) Aluminium: \( 200(23.1\times10^{-6})(5) = 0.0231\ \mathrm{mm} = 23.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) \( 11.5/46 = 0.25 \) — a quarter of the tolerance band.

(4) \( 11.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 0.0115\ \mathrm{mm} \div 25.4 = 0.00045\ \mathrm{in} \), that is 0.45 thou.

(5) An aluminium part on a steel gauge, both at 25°C, leaves the difference: \( 23.1 - 11.5 = 11.6\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

Answer: 11.5 µm steel and 23.1 µm aluminium; the steel error is 25% of an IT7 band, or 0.45 thou; measuring aluminium with a steel gauge leaves 11.6 µm. Sanity check: the differential case is the one worth remembering, because it survives every improvement to the instrument — a perfect gauge of the wrong material still reports 11.6 µm of temperature. It also explains why gauge blocks are specified in the same material as the work where precision matters, and why the reference temperature is written into the definition of a dimension rather than left to the inspector. A quarter of the tolerance band spent before measuring is the practical reason inspection rooms are air-conditioned.

quiz.q:
Is the check good enough to make the call?

Problem. A feature has a tolerance band of 46 µm. Three candidate checks are offered: (a) the micrometer above, uncertainty 1.03 µm per reading; (b) a vernier caliper with 20 µm resolution and a repeatability of 15 µm; (c) a comparator reading against the gauge block, uncertainty 2.0 µm. Apply the 4:1 rule — the tolerance should be at least four times the measurement uncertainty — and say which checks are fit for the job.
quiz.solution:
Solution. The rule asks for \( T/u \ge 4 \), i.e. \( u \le 46/4 = 11.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(a) \( 46/1.03 = 44.7 \) ✓ comfortably fit — provided the bias is corrected, since the 5.2 µm offset is not part of \( s \).

(b) \( 46/15 = 3.1 \) ✗ below 4: the caliper's scatter alone eats a third of the band, and its 20 µm resolution is itself nearly half the tolerance.

(c) \( 46/2.0 = 23 \) ✓ fit.

Answer: (a) and (c) are fit for purpose, (b) is not. Sanity check: case (a) carries the lesson's trap. Judged on repeatability alone the micrometer looks like the best of the three, and used uncorrected it would report every part 5.2 µm oversize — more than the entire uncertainty budget the rule allows. The 4:1 rule is a statement about uncertainty, and an uncorrected bias is not uncertainty, it is error. A gauge that has been characterised and not corrected is worse than one that has not been characterised, because the number is now trusted.

quiz.q: An instrument's resolution is
choices: how close its readings are to the true value
the smallest change it can display
quiz.solution: Resolution is a property of the display and nothing more. A micrometer resolving to 1 µm can read 5 µm high all day, as the worked example does. Closeness to truth is accuracy, the spread of repeats is precision, and all three are independent — which is why a specification quoting only resolution tells you almost nothing about whether an instrument can do a job.

quiz.q: Ten repeated readings are averaged instead of one being taken. This improves
choices: precision of the mean, by \( \sqrt{10} \), leaving bias untouched
quiz.solution: \( u(\bar{x}) = s/\sqrt{n} \), so ten readings tighten the mean from 1.03 to 0.33 µm. Bias is systematic: every one of the ten readings carries the same 5.2 µm offset, so their average carries it too. More readings of a wrong ruler are still wrong, and this is the single most useful thing to understand about repetition.

quiz.q: Traceability means that a measurement
choices: was made by a certified technician
links to a national standard through an unbroken chain of calibrations, each with a stated uncertainty
is recorded in a quality system
quiz.solution: It is the chain, and the uncertainty stated at every link. Each step adds uncertainty rather than removing it, which is why a working gauge is calibrated against a reference several times better than itself. A record in a quality system is evidence of traceability, not traceability; a technician's certification is about competence, which is a different requirement.

quiz.q: A calibration certificate gives a result but states no uncertainty. It is
choices: acceptable if the laboratory is accredited
not a calibration certificate — the uncertainty is part of the result
acceptable if a coverage factor is implied
quiz.solution: A measurement result without an uncertainty is not a result, because nothing can be judged against it: you cannot apply a 4:1 rule, cannot decide conformity near a limit, and cannot pass traceability down another link. Accreditation is what makes a stated uncertainty credible; it does not substitute for stating one.

quiz.q: Dimensional metrology defines length at
quiz.solution: 20°C is part of what a dimension means, not a convenience. A 200 mm steel part at 25°C is 11.5 µm longer than its defined size — a quarter of an IT7 band — and an aluminium one is 23.1 µm longer. Without a defined reference temperature, a drawing dimension would not be a single number.

quiz.q: An aluminium part is measured with a steel gauge, both at 25°C. The residual error is
choices: 11.6 µm per 200 mm, from the difference in expansion coefficients
quiz.solution: Both expand, so part of the error cancels — but not all of it, because the coefficients differ: \( (23.1-11.5)\times10^{-6}(200)(5) = 11.6\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). This differential term survives any improvement to the instrument, which is why gauges are specified in the same material as the work when precision matters, and why "both are at the same temperature" is not the reassurance it sounds like.

quiz.q: The 4:1 rule requires that the tolerance being checked is at least four times the
quiz.solution: It is a ratio of tolerance to uncertainty, so the whole measurement process is in scope, not just the display. It also does not license an uncorrected bias: a bias is a known error and belongs corrected, not absorbed into an uncertainty budget. The worked micrometer passes the rule at 44:1 on scatter and would still report every part 5.2 µm oversize.

quiz.q: A part is carried straight from a machining centre to the inspection room and measured immediately. The measurement
choices: is valid, because the room is at 20°C
reflects the part's temperature history rather than its size
is valid if the instrument is calibrated
is only affected for aluminium parts
quiz.solution: The room being at 20°C says nothing about the part, which arrives carrying the heat of the cut. Soak time is a real requirement, not a ritual: until the part reaches the reference temperature, \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \) is measuring how recently it was machined. A calibrated instrument reports that thermal state faithfully, which is precisely the problem.

1.kuwait:
Applied case — the shaft batch that failed at the customer and passed at the works. A batch of 200 mm shafts was inspected against a 46 µm diameter tolerance, passed, shipped, and rejected on receipt as oversize. Both parties re-measured, both were confident, and the readings differed by about 5 µm consistently — not randomly, which is the detail that solved it.

A consistent difference is a bias, and bias belongs to an instrument rather than to a process. Checking the works micrometer against a gauge block certified at 25.0000 mm with \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) gave ten readings averaging 25.0052 mm: the instrument read 5.2 µm high, with a repeatability of only 1.03 µm. Its scatter was excellent, which is why nobody had suspected it — repeated measurements agreed beautifully with each other and consistently with nothing else. Against a 46 µm band, a 5.2 µm offset consumes 11% of the tolerance and moves the whole batch toward one limit.

Two practices follow. Repeatability checks are not calibration: agreeing with yourself is the one thing a biased instrument does perfectly, so an instrument must periodically be compared with a traceable reference and not merely with itself. And when two parties disagree consistently rather than randomly, the argument is about a gauge, not about a process — the fastest route to the answer is for both to measure the same certified artefact, which takes minutes and settles what weeks of re-inspection will not.
1.recap:
• Resolution is what the display can show, precision is agreement among repeats, bias is a systematic offset, and accuracy needs small bias and small scatter.
  • The worked micrometer reads 25.0052 mm on a 25.0000 mm block with \( s=1.03\ \mu\mathrm{m} \): precise and inaccurate, the combination that survives careless checking.
  • \( u(\bar{x})=s/\sqrt{n} \): ten readings tighten the mean to 0.33 µm and leave the 5.2 µm bias exactly where it was.
  • Judge a check against its reference: a 5.2 µm bias against a block certified to 0.2 µm is 26:1, so the error is the instrument's.
  • Traceability is an unbroken chain of calibrations to a national standard, each with a stated uncertainty; uncertainty accumulates downward and never shrinks.
  • A certificate states measurand, reference standard, result with uncertainty and coverage factor, and conditions. A result without an uncertainty is not a result.
  • Dimensional metrology is defined at 20°C, and \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \) is not optional arithmetic.
  • A 200 mm steel part at 25°C is 11.5 µm long — a quarter of an IT7 band; in aluminium, 23.1 µm.
  • Measuring aluminium with a steel gauge leaves the differential 11.6 µm, which no instrument quality removes.
  • The 4:1 rule compares tolerance with uncertainty; a known bias belongs corrected, not absorbed into the budget.

2.lecture:
§1 · The instruments, ranked honestly

A workshop's dimensional instruments are not interchangeable, and the ranking is not about price. It is about how each one turns a physical contact into a number, and where that conversion leaks.

A vernier or digital caliper is the general-purpose instrument: wide range, quick, and the least accurate of the set for reasons that are structural rather than fixable. A micrometer trades range for accuracy, measuring over perhaps 25 mm per instrument with a calibrated screw. A dial indicator measures nothing absolutely at all — it reads differences against a set reference, which is why it is the natural instrument for runout, flatness and comparison work. Gauge blocks are not instruments but embodied lengths, the artefacts everything else is set against. And a comparator is a dial indicator given a rigid stand and a gauge-block reference, which is how a workshop reaches micrometre work without buying a laboratory.

The order matters because the usual failure is to reach for the convenient instrument and then believe its last digit. A caliper displaying 0.01 mm invites a confidence its construction does not support.

§2 · Abbe's principle, and why a caliper cannot win

In 1890 Ernst Abbe stated the rule that still separates good instrument design from bad: the line along which you measure should be collinear with the instrument's scale. When it is not, the perpendicular distance between them — the Abbe offset — turns any angular error into a length error.

Key relation — Abbe error

\[ \varepsilon = h\tan\theta \approx h\theta \]

\( h \) is the Abbe offset and \( \theta \) the angular error. The error is first order in \( \theta \) and proportional to \( h \) — so it vanishes only when \( h = 0 \).

A caliper measures at the jaw tips while its scale runs along the beam, perhaps 40 mm away. Tilt the jaws by a tenth of a degree — an angle no operator can see, easily produced by measuring-force rock in the slide — and \( \varepsilon = 40\tan(0.1^\circ) = 69.8\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

A micrometer has its anvil and spindle on the axis of the screw that does the measuring, so \( h \approx 0 \). The same tilt leaves only a cosine error, \( L(1-\cos\theta) \), which is second order: \( 25(1-\cos 0.1^\circ) = 0.038\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The micrometer is better by a factor of 1833 for the same misalignment, and it is the geometry that earns it, not the workmanship.

The orders of magnitude in \( \theta \) are the part worth carrying. Double the tilt and the caliper's Abbe error doubles, from 69.8 to 139.6 µm, while the micrometer's cosine error quadruples — from 0.038 to 0.152 µm, which is still nothing. A first-order error with a lever on it beats a second-order error every time, and that is the whole argument for Abbe's principle.

§3 · Gauge blocks: length you can put on the bench

Gauge blocks are hardened, lapped rectangular blocks whose length between opposite faces is certified. Their surfaces are flat and fine enough to wring — pressed and twisted together they adhere strongly, and a stack behaves as one block of the summed length.

Building a stack follows one rule: work from the finest decimal place and eliminate it first. For 41.275 mm from a standard set — take 1.005 to clear the third decimal, then 1.27 to clear the second and first, then 8.0, then 31.0. Four blocks, and the check is trivial: \( 1.005+1.27+8.0+31.0 = 41.275 \).

Use as few blocks as the set allows. Every wrung interface contributes a small uncertainty and a small risk of contamination, so a four-block stack is better than a seven-block one of the same length. Blocks are also the reason the previous lesson's temperature discussion is not academic: they are the reference the whole shop is traceable to, and they are steel.

§4 · Measuring force, contact, and the errors of use

Every contact instrument deforms what it measures and deforms itself. A micrometer's ratchet or friction thimble exists to make that deformation repeatable rather than to make it small: a fixed measuring force means a fixed elastic compression at the contact, which becomes part of the calibration instead of part of the scatter. An operator who bypasses the ratchet and "feels" the fit has replaced a controlled force with a variable one, and has converted a bias into a scatter — which, as Lesson 1 showed, is the harder of the two to detect.

The other errors of use are worth naming because they are all systematic:

  • Parallax on any analogue scale — read square to the dial, not at an angle.
  • Anvil wear on a micrometer, checked by closing it on nothing and confirming zero, and by checking at several points in the range rather than only at zero.
  • Dirt and burrs, which are not small at this scale: a fingerprint is around 1 µm thick and a wrung interface is cleaner than that.
  • Heat from the hand, which is why blocks and micrometers are handled with a cloth or by their insulating pads for precise work — Lesson 1's \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \) does not care that the heat came from an operator.

None of these is exotic and none is eliminated by buying a better instrument. They are the reason an instrument's specification is an upper bound on its performance rather than a description of it.
2.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Bias and precision (Lesson 1) — the distinction that decides which errors of use matter and how they show up.
  • Thermal error (Lesson 1) — \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \), applied here to hand heat and to steel gauge blocks.
  • Small-angle behaviour (Engineering Mathematics I L11) — why \( \tan\theta\approx\theta \) is first order and \( 1-\cos\theta \) is second.
  • Tolerances and IT grades (Engineering Drawing & CAD L6) — the bands these instrument errors are spent against.
  • Elastic contact (Strength of Materials L1) — why a measuring force must be controlled rather than merely light.

quiz.q:
Abbe error against cosine error

Problem. A caliper measures at jaw tips 40 mm from its scale; a micrometer measures a 25 mm length on the axis of its screw. Both are tilted by 0.1°. Find each instrument's error, their ratio, and then find both errors again at 0.2°. State how each error scales with tilt.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Caliper, Abbe error with \( h = 40 \) mm: \( \varepsilon = 40\tan(0.1^\circ) = 40(0.0017453) = 0.06981\ \mathrm{mm} = 69.8\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) Micrometer, \( h \approx 0 \), so only cosine error remains: \( \varepsilon = 25(1-\cos 0.1^\circ) = 25(1.523\times10^{-6}) = 3.81\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.038\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) Ratio \( = 69.8/0.0381 = 1833 \).

(4) At 0.2°: caliper \( 40\tan(0.2^\circ) = 139.6\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); micrometer \( 25(1-\cos 0.2^\circ) = 0.152\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(5) The Abbe error doubled (linear in \( \theta \)); the cosine error quadrupled (quadratic).

Answer: 69.8 µm against 0.038 µm, a ratio of 1833; at twice the tilt, 139.6 and 0.152 µm. Sanity check: the scaling is the real result. A first-order error multiplied by a 40 mm lever is in a different category from a second-order error with no lever, and no amount of manufacturing quality in the caliper closes the gap — it is decided by where the scale sits relative to the jaws. That is why Abbe's principle is an instrument-design rule and not an operating instruction, and why a caliper's last displayed digit should be treated as decoration on anything tighter than a few hundredths.

quiz.q:
Building a gauge block stack (with a US customary check)

Problem. Build 41.275 mm from a standard metric set containing 1.005, then 1.01–1.49 in 0.01 steps, 0.5–9.5 in 0.5 steps, and 10–100 in 10 steps. Use as few blocks as possible and state the rule you followed. Then express the stack height in inches, and say why using seven blocks instead of four would be worse.
quiz.solution:
Solution. Work from the finest decimal and eliminate it first.

(1) The third decimal is 5, cleared only by the 1.005 block. Remainder \( 41.275 - 1.005 = 40.270 \).

(2) The 0.07 and 0.2 are cleared together by 1.27 from the hundredths series. Remainder \( 40.270 - 1.27 = 39.000 \).

(3) The 9 is cleared by 8.0 plus the 31.0 — taking 8.0 leaves 31.000, which the tens series supplies directly.

(4) Stack: \( 1.005 + 1.27 + 8.0 + 31.0 = 41.275\ \mathrm{mm} \) ✓, four blocks.

(5) \( 41.275/25.4 = 1.6250\ \mathrm{in} \) exactly.

Answer: 1.005 + 1.27 + 8.0 + 31.0 mm, four blocks; 1.6250 in. Sanity check: the arithmetic check is trivial and should always be done — the sum must be exact, not close. Fewer blocks is better because each wrung interface adds a small uncertainty and one more opportunity for a trapped particle; a seven-block stack has nearly twice the interfaces of a four-block one for no benefit. The inch value coming out exact is a coincidence of this number, not a rule.

quiz.q:
Is the caliper fit for the tolerance?

Problem. A 25 mm shaft carries an IT7 tolerance of 21 µm. The workshop proposes to inspect it with the caliper above, whose jaws can tilt by up to 0.1° in normal use. Apply the 4:1 rule from Lesson 1 and decide. Then say what a micrometer would give, and what the correct instrument choice is.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The 4:1 rule asks for \( u \le T/4 = 21/4 = 5.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) The caliper's Abbe error alone is 69.8 µm — not an uncertainty contribution but a single error term, and it is \( 69.8/21 = 3.3 \) times the entire tolerance band.

(3) The micrometer's cosine error is 0.038 µm, which is \( 0.2\% \) of the 21 µm band and utterly negligible; its uncertainty will be dominated by other terms such as the 0.2 µm of its setting standard.

(4) The caliper is not merely outside the 4:1 rule — it cannot resolve the tolerance at all. The micrometer is the correct instrument, and for a production run a comparator set against a gauge block stack would be faster and no worse.

Answer: the caliper is unfit by a factor of more than thirteen against the 4:1 rule; use a micrometer, or a comparator for a run. Sanity check: the comparison is worth stating carefully, because the caliper's Abbe error is a worst case rather than a value present at every measurement — a careful operator will often do far better. That is exactly what makes it dangerous: an error that is sometimes 70 µm and sometimes near zero is invisible in a repeatability check and shows up as inexplicable scatter between operators. An instrument whose error depends on technique has converted a design fault into a personnel problem.

quiz.q: Abbe's principle states that the measuring line should be
choices: at the centre of the workpiece
quiz.solution: Collinear — that is, with zero offset between the axis you measure along and the scale that does the measuring. Where an offset \( h \) exists, any angular error \( \theta \) becomes a length error \( h\tan\theta \). It is a rule about instrument geometry, so it is satisfied or violated at the design stage and cannot be fixed by careful use.

quiz.q: Abbe error is first order in the tilt angle, which means that doubling the tilt
quiz.solution: \( \varepsilon = h\tan\theta \approx h\theta \), so the error scales linearly: 69.8 µm at 0.1° becomes 139.6 at 0.2°. Cosine error, \( L(1-\cos\theta) \), is the second-order one and quadruples over the same change — from 0.038 to 0.152 µm, which is still negligible. The difference in order, multiplied by the offset, is the whole argument.

quiz.q: A micrometer suffers far less tilt error than a caliper mainly because
choices: its measuring axis is collinear with its scale, so the Abbe offset is near zero
quiz.solution: The anvil and spindle sit on the axis of the measuring screw, so \( h\approx0 \) and the first-order term vanishes, leaving only second-order cosine error. Workmanship matters for other error sources, and the ratchet fixes the measuring force rather than the geometry — but the factor of 1833 against the caliper is bought by where the scale is, not by how well it is cut.

quiz.q: Gauge blocks wring together in order to
choices: behave as a single block of the summed length
quiz.solution: Wrung blocks adhere strongly enough that the stack behaves as one artefact of the summed length, which is what makes a set of a few dozen blocks able to embody thousands of lengths. Each interface does add a small uncertainty, which is why a stack uses as few blocks as the set allows — four for 41.275 mm rather than seven.

quiz.q: When building a gauge block stack, you start by choosing the block that
quiz.solution: Eliminate the finest decimal first, because only one or two blocks in the set can supply it — the 1.005 for the third decimal in 41.275 mm. Working downward from the largest block leaves a remainder the fine series may be unable to make exactly. The check at the end is arithmetic and must be exact: \( 1.005+1.27+8.0+31.0 = 41.275 \).

quiz.q: A micrometer's ratchet exists to
choices: make the measuring force repeatable, so contact deformation becomes part of the calibration
quiz.solution: Every contact instrument deforms the part and itself; a fixed force makes that deformation a fixed, repeatable amount that calibration absorbs. An operator who bypasses the ratchet and feels the fit replaces a controlled force with a variable one and converts a bias into scatter — which Lesson 1 showed is the harder of the two to notice. Protection from damage is a side benefit, not the reason.

quiz.q: A dial indicator is best described as an instrument that measures
quiz.solution: It reads displacement from wherever it was zeroed, which is why it is the natural instrument for runout, flatness and comparison work, and why it is useless on its own for an absolute size. Give it a rigid stand and a gauge-block reference and it becomes a comparator — the standard route to micrometre-level work without a metrology laboratory.

quiz.q: An instrument whose error depends heavily on operator technique is dangerous because
choices: the error is invisible in a repeatability check and appears as scatter between operators
quiz.solution: A single operator repeating their own technique will repeat their own error, so the instrument looks precise. The variation only appears when a second operator measures the same part — which is why Lesson 10's gauge R&R study separates repeatability (one operator) from reproducibility (between operators), and why a caliper with a 70 µm worst-case Abbe error can pass an informal check and still fail in production.

2.kuwait:
Applied case — the bore that two inspectors could not agree on. A 25 mm bore with a 21 µm tolerance was checked by two inspectors on the same shift using the same digital caliper. One passed the batch, the other rejected roughly a third of it. The caliper was sent for calibration, came back within specification, and the disagreement continued.

The calibration certificate was not wrong; it was answering a different question. A caliper's jaws sit about 40 mm from its scale, so a tilt of a tenth of a degree — produced by nothing more than how firmly each inspector held the slide — contributes \( 40\tan(0.1^\circ) = 69.8\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). That is 3.3 times the entire tolerance band, and it is technique-dependent, so each inspector repeated their own reading faithfully and the two of them differed. Calibration checks an instrument against a standard under controlled conditions; it cannot certify a measuring process that includes a 40 mm lever on operator grip.

Two practices follow. Instrument selection is part of the inspection method and belongs on the inspection sheet with the tolerance in view — a 21 µm band calls for a micrometer or a comparator set against blocks, and no caliper of any price is a candidate. And when two inspectors disagree while one instrument passes calibration, the question to ask is not "which is right" but "what in this method depends on who is holding it" — which is the question a gauge R&R study (Lesson 10) is built to answer.
2.recap:
• Calipers are wide-range and least accurate, micrometers trade range for accuracy, dial indicators measure differences only, gauge blocks are embodied length, and a comparator is an indicator plus a stand plus a block.
  • Abbe's principle: the measuring line should be collinear with the scale. Any offset \( h \) turns an angular error into \( \varepsilon = h\tan\theta \).
  • Abbe error is first order in tilt; cosine error \( L(1-\cos\theta) \), all that remains when \( h=0 \), is second order.
  • A caliper with a 40 mm offset tilted 0.1° gives 69.8 µm; a micrometer at the same tilt gives 0.038 µm — a factor of 1833, bought by geometry rather than workmanship.
  • Double the tilt and the caliper error doubles while the micrometer error quadruples from a number that was already negligible.
  • Gauge blocks wring so a stack acts as one length; build from the finest decimal first, and use as few blocks as possible — 41.275 mm as 1.005 + 1.27 + 8.0 + 31.0.
  • Every wrung interface adds uncertainty and a contamination risk, so four blocks beat seven for the same length.
  • A ratchet fixes the measuring force so contact deformation is repeatable and calibration can absorb it; feeling the fit converts a bias into scatter.
  • Parallax, anvil wear, dirt and hand heat are all systematic and none is fixed by buying a better instrument — a specification is an upper bound on performance, not a description of it.
  • An error that depends on technique passes a repeatability check and fails between operators, which is what gauge R&R exists to expose.

3.lecture:
§1 · A result without an uncertainty is not a result

Lesson 1 ended on that claim; this lesson makes it operational. An uncertainty is the width of the interval that can reasonably be attributed to the measurand — not a mistake, not a tolerance, and not a guess. It is computed, and the computation is a budget: list everything that could move the answer, put a standard deviation on each, and combine them.

The vocabulary trips people at the first step. Type A and Type B classify how a component was evaluated, not what kind of error it is. Type A means evaluated by statistics on repeated observations; Type B means evaluated by any other means — a calibration certificate, a manufacturer's specification, the resolution of a display, or documented judgement. A systematic effect can be Type A and a random one Type B. The distinction that people import from elsewhere, random versus systematic, is a different axis entirely and does not appear in the arithmetic.

§2 · Building the budget

Each component enters as a standard uncertainty, which is a standard deviation. Getting it there depends on what you know about the component.

Key relations — converting to standard uncertainty

\[ u = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\ \text{(mean of \(n\) repeats)},\qquad u = \frac{U}{k}\ \text{(certificate)},\qquad u = \frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\ \text{(rectangular, half-width \(a\))} \]

The rectangular divisor applies when a value is known only to lie within limits with no reason to prefer the middle — the usual case for a display resolution or a temperature band.

Take the micrometer of Lesson 1, calibrated against the 25 mm block. Four components:

  • Repeatability (Type A): ten readings gave \( s = 1.03\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), and the result is their mean, so \( u = 1.03/\sqrt{10} = 0.327\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).
  • Display resolution (Type B): 1 µm steps, so the true value lies within \( \pm0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) of what is shown; rectangular, \( u = 0.5/\sqrt{3} = 0.289\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).
  • Temperature (Type B): the room is held to \( \pm1\ \mathrm{K} \), and \( 25\ \mathrm{mm}\times11.5\times10^{-6}\times1\ \mathrm{K} = 0.288\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) of half-width; rectangular, \( u = 0.166\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).
  • Reference block (Type B): certificate says \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( k=2 \), so \( u = 0.10\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).
Key relation — combining and expanding

\[ u_c=\sqrt{\textstyle\sum u_i^2},\qquad U=k\,u_c\ \ (k=2 \approx 95\%) \]

Independent components add in quadrature, so the largest dominates and the small ones almost vanish.

\( u_c=\sqrt{0.327^2+0.289^2+0.166^2+0.100^2}=0.477\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), and \( U = 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The calibration therefore reports a correction of \( -5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) with an uncertainty of \( 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( k=2 \).

§3 · Reading the budget, which is the point of writing it

The single number \( U \) is what goes on the certificate; the ranking is what the budget is actually for. Because components add in quadrature, their variance shares are what matter: repeatability 47%, resolution 37%, temperature 12%, block 4%.

That ordering is a spending plan. Buying a block certified ten times better would improve \( u_c \) by less than a tenth of a per cent, because 4% of the variance cannot be worth much. Taking more readings attacks the biggest term — but quadrupling them to 40 only reduces \( U \) from 0.95 to 0.77 µm, a 19% gain for four times the work, because \( s/\sqrt{n} \) improves as a square root and the display's resolution is waiting underneath at 0.289 µm. Beyond that point the only remaining moves are a finer display or a different instrument.

The budget also settles whether the bias is real. The measured offset is 5.2 µm against an expanded uncertainty of 0.95 µm — a factor of 5.5 — so it is not an artefact of the calibration, and it should be corrected rather than ignored. Had the bias come out at, say, 0.6 µm, the honest statement would have been that no bias was detected at this uncertainty.

§4 · From certificate to decision: intervals, guard bands, and the bad day

Calibration is not an event but a cycle. The interval is set by how the instrument actually behaves — its drift history, how hard it is used, and what it decides — not by a number copied from a supplier's leaflet. Instruments that pass comfortably every time earn a longer interval; one that drifts earns a shorter one, and the evidence for either is the calibration history.

Using the certificate to accept a part introduces a second decision. A measured value sitting exactly on the tolerance limit is a coin toss, because the uncertainty straddles it. A guard band resolves this by accepting only within limits pulled in by \( U \): on a 21 µm tolerance with \( U = 0.95 \), accepting only within \( 21 - 2(0.95) = 19.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) of band gives a confident pass, at the cost of rejecting some good parts. Which risk to carry is a commercial decision, and it belongs written down in a decision rule rather than settled per-inspector.

Finally, the case everyone hopes to avoid. When an instrument is found out of tolerance at calibration, the problem is not the instrument — it is every measurement made with it since the last good calibration, all of which are now suspect. That is why calibration records identify which instrument measured what, and why the interval matters commercially: it bounds how much work an out-of-tolerance finding puts back in question. A shop that cannot answer "what did this gauge measure since March" has a records problem that a calibration contract does not solve.
3.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Bias, precision and the standard error (Lesson 1) — the ten readings reused here as the Type A component.
  • Thermal error (Lesson 1) — \( \Delta L=L\alpha\Delta T \), entering the budget as a temperature term.
  • Instrument resolution (Lesson 2) — which becomes a rectangular contribution rather than a rounding nuisance.
  • Variance of a sum (Engineering Statistics L4) — why independent contributions add in quadrature and not linearly.
  • Normal and uniform distributions (Engineering Statistics L3) — the source of the \( k=2 \) and \( \sqrt{3} \) divisors.

Glossary

TermEquationWhen to use

Type B evaluationcertificates, specs, judgementEvaluated by any other means — not "systematic".
Rectangular\( u=a/\sqrt3 \)Known only to lie within \( \pm a \); resolution, temperature bands.

quiz.q:
A micrometer calibration budget, end to end

Problem. Build the uncertainty budget for the Lesson 1 calibration. The components are: repeatability, \( s = 1.03\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) over ten readings, the result being their mean; display resolution 1 µm; room temperature held to \( \pm1\ \mathrm{K} \) on a 25 mm steel block (\( \alpha = 11.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} \)); and a reference block certified at \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), \( k=2 \). Find each standard uncertainty, the combined and expanded uncertainty, and state the reported result given a measured bias of \( +5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Repeatability, Type A: \( u_1 = s/\sqrt{n} = 1.03/\sqrt{10} = 0.327\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) Resolution, Type B, rectangular with half-width 0.5 µm: \( u_2 = 0.5/\sqrt{3} = 0.289\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) Temperature, Type B: half-width \( 25(11.5\times10^{-6})(1) = 0.2875\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), rectangular, so \( u_3 = 0.2875/\sqrt{3} = 0.166\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(4) Reference block, Type B: \( u_4 = U/k = 0.2/2 = 0.100\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(5) \( u_c = \sqrt{0.327^2+0.289^2+0.166^2+0.100^2} = \sqrt{0.1069+0.0834+0.0276+0.0100} = \sqrt{0.2278} = 0.477\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(6) \( U = 2u_c = 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

Answer: the micrometer requires a correction of \( -5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), with an expanded uncertainty of \( 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( k=2 \). Sanity check: the bias is 5.5 times the expanded uncertainty, so it is unambiguously real and belongs corrected rather than noted. Note also that the four components span a factor of only 3.3 between largest and smallest, yet in quadrature the smallest contributes 4% of the variance against the largest's 47% — quadrature punishes small terms hard, which is why chasing them is almost always wasted effort.

quiz.q:
What should we spend money on?

Problem. Using the budget above, compute each component's share of the total variance. Then evaluate two proposals: (a) buy a reference block certified ten times better, and (b) increase the repeat count from 10 to 40. Give the new \( U \) in each case and say which is worth doing.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Variance shares, \( u_i^2/u_c^2 \) with \( u_c^2 = 0.2278 \):

repeatability \( 0.1069/0.2278 = 46.9\% \); resolution \( 0.0834/0.2278 = 36.6\% \); temperature \( 0.0276/0.2278 = 12.1\% \); block \( 0.0100/0.2278 = 4.4\% \).

(2) Proposal (a): a block ten times better gives \( u_4 = 0.010 \), so \( u_c = \sqrt{0.2278-0.0100+0.0001} = \sqrt{0.2179} = 0.4668 \) and \( U = 0.93\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) — a 2% improvement for a large cost.

(3) Proposal (b): \( u_1 = 1.03/\sqrt{40} = 0.163 \), so \( u_c = \sqrt{0.0266+0.0834+0.0276+0.0100} = \sqrt{0.1476} = 0.384 \) and \( U = 0.77\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) — a 19% improvement for four times the measuring effort.

Answer: shares 46.9 / 36.6 / 12.1 / 4.4 per cent; the better block buys 2% and the extra readings buy 19%. Take the readings if either. Sanity check: the diminishing return in (b) is the instructive part. Quadrupling \( n \) halves only the repeatability term, and once it has fallen to 0.163 the display resolution at 0.289 is the largest contributor — a term that no number of repeats can touch. A budget is worth rebuilding after any improvement, because the thing to fix next is rarely the thing you just fixed.

quiz.q:
Guard banding a conformity decision (with a US customary check)

Problem. A 25 mm feature carries a 21 µm tolerance and is measured with the calibrated micrometer, \( U = 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). (a) Find the guard-banded acceptance band if both limits are pulled in by \( U \). (b) A part measures 0.4 µm inside the upper limit — state the correct decision. (c) Give the guard-banded band in thousandths of an inch. (d) Say what changes if the same feature is inspected with the Lesson 2 caliper.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (a) Pulling each limit in by \( U \) removes \( 2U \) from the band: \( 21 - 2(0.95) = 19.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(b) The part sits 0.4 µm inside the limit, which is less than \( U = 0.95 \). It is inside the tolerance as measured but inside the guard band's rejected zone: conformity cannot be demonstrated, so under a guarded-acceptance rule it is not accepted.

(c) \( 19.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 0.0191\ \mathrm{mm} \div 25.4 = 0.00075\ \mathrm{in} \), that is 0.75 thou, against a 0.83 thou tolerance.

(d) The caliper's worst-case Abbe error alone is 69.8 µm — more than three times the whole tolerance. There is no guard band to compute: \( T - 2U \) would be negative, meaning no measured value could demonstrate conformity at all.

Answer: a 19.1 µm acceptance band (0.75 thou); the part at 0.4 µm inside is not accepted; with the caliper the decision is impossible. Sanity check: part (d) is the useful one. A negative guard band is the arithmetic telling you the measurement cannot support the decision being asked of it — the same verdict the 4:1 rule gave in Lesson 1, arrived at from the other direction. Note also that guard banding protects the customer by rejecting some good parts; pushing the band outward instead protects the supplier and ships some bad ones. Neither is neutral, which is why the choice belongs in a written decision rule rather than in an inspector's judgement.

quiz.q: Type A and Type B uncertainty components are distinguished by
choices: whether they are large or small
whether they appear on a certificate
quiz.solution: Type A means evaluated by statistics on repeated observations; Type B means evaluated by any other means — a certificate, a specification, a display resolution, or documented judgement. Random versus systematic is a different axis: a systematic effect can be evaluated statistically and a random one from a specification. Nothing in the combination arithmetic depends on the classification at all.

quiz.q: A display resolves to 1 µm. Its contribution to the uncertainty budget is
choices: zero, since it is not an error
quiz.solution: The true value lies within half a count either side of what is shown, with no reason to prefer the middle, so it is a rectangular distribution of half-width 0.5 µm and its standard uncertainty is \( a/\sqrt3 = 0.289\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Using the half-width directly overstates it by 73%; using the full count overstates it by more than three times.

quiz.q: A certificate states \( U = 0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( k = 2 \). The standard uncertainty to enter in a budget is
quiz.solution: \( u = U/k = 0.2/2 = 0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The coverage factor has to be undone before combining, because budgets combine standard uncertainties and are expanded only once at the end. Entering the expanded value directly double-counts the coverage factor and inflates the final \( U \).

quiz.q: Independent uncertainty components are combined
quiz.solution: Variances add for independent contributions, so the standard uncertainties add in quadrature. The practical consequence is that quadrature punishes small terms severely: in the worked budget the smallest component is only 3.3 times smaller than the largest, yet contributes 4% of the variance against 47%. Taking the largest alone would understate \( u_c \) by about a third here.

quiz.q: In the worked budget, repeatability contributes 47% of the variance and the reference block 4%. Buying a block ten times better would
quiz.solution: Removing almost all of a 4% share leaves \( u_c=\sqrt{0.2278-0.0100} = 0.467 \) against 0.477, so \( U \) falls from 0.95 to 0.93 µm — about 2%. It is not literally zero, but it is money spent on the smallest term in the budget. That ranking is the main reason to write a budget rather than merely quote its total.

quiz.q: Quadrupling the number of repeat readings from 10 to 40 reduces the worked \( U \) from 0.95 to 0.77 µm. The reason the gain is only 19% is that
choices: \( s/\sqrt{n} \) improves only as a square root, and the resolution term then dominates
temperature drifts over a longer session
quiz.solution: Four times the readings halve the repeatability term, from 0.327 to 0.163 — but the display resolution sits underneath at 0.289 and is untouched by repeating. Once the biggest term has been beaten below another, further effort on it buys almost nothing. Rebuild the budget after any improvement: what to fix next is rarely what you just fixed.

quiz.q: A measured value sits 0.4 µm inside a tolerance limit, with \( U = 0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Under a guarded-acceptance rule the part is
choices: accepted, since it is inside the limit
not accepted, because conformity cannot be demonstrated within the uncertainty
quiz.solution: The uncertainty straddles the limit, so the measurement cannot demonstrate conformity. Guarded acceptance pulls the acceptance limits in by \( U \) — a 21 µm tolerance becomes a 19.1 µm acceptance band — and protects the customer at the cost of rejecting some genuinely good parts. Re-measuring until a favourable reading appears is not a decision rule; it is selecting from noise.

quiz.q: An instrument is found out of tolerance at its calibration. The most serious consequence is that
choices: its calibration interval must be shortened
every measurement made with it since the last good calibration is suspect
the calibration laboratory must be audited
quiz.solution: The instrument can be adjusted or replaced in an afternoon; the work it has already passed cannot. Everything measured since the last good calibration is now in question, which is why records must link instruments to the parts they measured, and why the calibration interval is a commercial decision as well as a technical one — it bounds how much work an out-of-tolerance finding puts back on the table.

3.kuwait:
Applied case — the better gauge block that changed nothing. An inspection department was asked to tighten its measurement uncertainty and responded by replacing its reference gauge blocks with a grade certified an order of magnitude better. The purchase was substantial, the certificates were impressive, and the reported uncertainty on the department's calibrations barely moved.

The budget said why, and the budget had never been written. Of the four components in a typical micrometer calibration — repeatability 0.327, resolution 0.289, temperature 0.166 and the block 0.100 µm — the block contributed 4.4% of the variance. Removing almost all of it took \( u_c \) from 0.477 to 0.467 µm and \( U \) from 0.95 to 0.93: a 2% improvement. Meanwhile repeatability at 46.9% and display resolution at 36.6% together held five-sixths of the variance, and neither had been touched. Quadrature is unforgiving that way — a component three times smaller than the leader carries a ninth of its weight.

Two practices follow. Write the budget before spending: it is an afternoon's arithmetic and it ranks every possible improvement by what it would actually buy, which no supplier's datasheet does. And rebuild it after each change, because the ranking moves — in this budget, taking four times as many readings would have been the right first move, and would then have left display resolution as the largest term and a finer instrument as the only remaining option.
3.recap:
• Uncertainty is a computed interval, not a mistake or a tolerance; a result without one cannot be used for a decision.
  • Type A and Type B classify how a component was evaluated — by statistics, or by any other means. It is not the random/systematic distinction.
  • Convert to standard uncertainty first: \( s/\sqrt n \) for a mean, \( U/k \) from a certificate, \( a/\sqrt3 \) for a rectangular half-width.
  • The worked micrometer budget: repeatability 0.327, resolution 0.289, temperature 0.166, block 0.100 µm.
  • \( u_c=\sqrt{\sum u_i^2}=0.477\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and \( U=2u_c=0.95\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); the reported result is a \( -5.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) correction with that uncertainty.
  • The bias is 5.5 times \( U \), so it is real and belongs corrected; a bias comparable with \( U \) would honestly be "none detected".
  • Variance shares are the spending plan: 46.9% repeatability, 36.6% resolution, 12.1% temperature, 4.4% block.
  • A ten-times-better block buys 2%; quadrupling the readings buys 19% and then leaves resolution dominant — rebuild the budget after every improvement.
  • Guard banding pulls acceptance limits in by \( U \): a 21 µm tolerance becomes a 19.1 µm band, protecting the customer and rejecting some good parts.
  • A negative guard band means the measurement cannot support the decision — the 4:1 rule of Lesson 1 arriving from the other direction.
  • An out-of-tolerance finding at calibration puts every measurement since the last good calibration in question, which is what records and intervals exist to bound.
